summary: Describes a tunnel broker that uses the Tunnel Setup Protocol (TSP) so a client can ask for a tunnel, for example IPv6 inside IPv4, and have the broker negotiate and configure it. TSP can also handle IPv4 NAT traversal using UDP, and suits mobile nodes that move between IPv4 and IPv6 networks. This is an experimental protocol, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: If your road has no bridge to a new town, a broker is like a helper who builds you a private tunnel to get there. You ask politely, and the helper sets up everything.

questions: what is the tunnel setup protocol
how does tunnel setup protocol work
what is ipv6 tunnel broker tsp
subtitle: A protocol to negotiate tunnels between mobile hosts and brokers.

tldr.problem: Hosts that lack IPv6 connectivity or are stuck behind IPv4 NATs need a way to request and configure tunnels on demand. Existing tunnel deployment required manual configuration or third-party relay servers, making it impractical for mobile nodes.
tldr.mechanism: The Tunnel Setup Protocol (TSP) uses XML messaging over TCP or UDP to let a client negotiate tunnel parameters with a broker. TSP detects NAT by comparing IP source addresses, selects the right tunnel type (IPv6-over-IPv4 or IPv6-over-UDP), assigns addresses and prefixes, and keeps the tunnel alive as the client moves.
tldr.outcome: Mobile hosts can automatically obtain and maintain IPv6 or IPv4 tunnels with address stability, even across network changes. The solution is flexible and extensible but experimental.

today: RFC 5572 is Experimental. TSP was implemented in some IPv6 tunnel brokers (notably in the Hexago Freenet6 service) and demonstrated the concept, but it did not become widely standardized. IPv6 transition preferences shifted toward other mechanisms like 6to4 and Teredo. However, TSP's principles remain relevant for mobile and multi-homed scenarios.

sections.title: The Tunnel Broker Model
sections.content:
The tunnel broker model separates three roles: a tunnel client (the host needing a tunnel), a tunnel server (the far end of the tunnel), and a tunnel broker (a service that negotiates on behalf of the server). The client application sends TSP requests to the broker to set up, update, or tear down tunnels.

Tunnels can carry IPv6 over IPv4 (useful for connecting to IPv6 networks from IPv4-only paths), IPv4 over IPv6 (for IPv4-dependent applications on IPv6-only networks), or IPv6 over UDP-over-IPv4 (to traverse NATs). The broker assigns IPv6 addresses or prefixes to the client and optionally records them in DNS.
sections.plainLanguage: A tunnel broker is like a post office helper. You tell them 'I need a tunnel to get IPv6', they figure out the best way through the network, and they set it up with a stable address.

sections.title: The Three Phases of TSP
sections.content:
TSP signaling has three phases. In the Authentication phase, the client and broker exchange protocol versions and capabilities, then authenticate using SASL (Simple Authentication and Security Layer). Either anonymous or challenge-response authentication is supported.

In the Command phase, the client sends an XML tunnel request describing the desired encapsulation, address family, and any options like prefix delegation or DNS registration. In the Response phase, the broker replies with an XML message containing the assigned addresses, prefixes, gateway information, and a tunnel acknowledgement.

After these phases succeed, the tunnel is established, and periodic keep-alive messages may be exchanged to maintain NAT mappings or session state.
sections.plainLanguage: First you say 'hello, can you help?', then you explain what you need, and finally the broker tells you 'here is your tunnel address'.

sections.title: TSP Signaling Transport
sections.content:
TSP messages are sent as XML over either TCP (port 3653) or UDP. TCP is simpler and reliable; UDP requires the client to add a reliability layer with sequence numbers and timestamps for retransmission. The choice of transport depends on the tunnel type: requests for IPv6-over-UDP tunnels must use UDP signaling so that the same NAT mapping is reused for both the TSP session and the tunnel itself.

When sent over UDP, each TSP packet begins with a 4-bit marker (0xF), a 28-bit sequence number, and a 32-bit timestamp, followed by the TSP data. The client retransmits unacknowledged packets with exponential backoff.
sections.plainLanguage: You can send requests to the broker over a reliable phone line (TCP) or a radio (UDP). If using radio, you number and time-stamp each message so you know when to repeat it.

sections.title: NAT Detection and Tunnel Selection
sections.content:
TSP includes a built-in NAT detection mechanism. When the client sends a UDP tunnel request, it includes its own source IPv4 address inside the message. The broker compares this address with the IP source address of the arriving packet. If they differ, one or more NATs are in the path.

When NAT is detected, the broker automatically selects IPv6-over-UDP encapsulation instead of plain IPv6-over-IPv4, because the UDP tunnel will use the same NAT mapping as the TSP signaling session. This means the tunnel traffic stays alive even after the TSP session ends, as long as keep-alive packets maintain the mapping.
sections.plainLanguage: The broker asks 'what address do you see yourself from?' If your answer doesn't match what the broker sees, it knows you're behind a blocker and picks a tunnel type that works through blockers.

sections.title: Handling Mobility and Address Stability
sections.content:
When a mobile host changes its IPv4 address (moving to a new network), the TSP client automatically reconnects to the broker and updates tunnel parameters. The crucial feature is address stability: if the user is authenticated, the broker reassigns the same IPv6 address or prefix, even though the underlying IPv4 address or tunnel encapsulation has changed. This stability is essential for applications that need a stable home address (email, DNS records, etc.).

Optional features include IPv6 prefix delegation (the client can distribute addresses to downstream hosts), DNS delegation (for reverse lookups), and routing protocol negotiation to handle more complex topologies.
sections.plainLanguage: When you move to a new town, the tunnel broker recognizes you by your user login and gives you a new tunnel, but keeps your stable home address. Apps don't notice you moved.
